Series::is_nonzero¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_nonzero() const

What It Does¶

Collapses a single-element Series to one bool: true if that one value is not equal to 0, false if it is.

“Single element” means numel() == 1 — a rank-0 scalar and a [1] (or [1, 1], …) vector both qualify. Anything with more than one value, and every empty Series, raises rather than guessing what you meant.

That strictness is the point. is_nonzero() is the safe way to turn a computed condition into a C++ bool for an if, precisely because it refuses a multi-value tensor instead of silently testing just the first element or the whole thing. When you do mean “are all values nonzero” or “is any value nonzero”, say so with all() or any() and then call is_nonzero() on that one-element result.

The comparison is exactly value != 0:

  • NaN != 0 is true, so is_nonzero() of NaN is true.

  • -0.0 == 0.0, so is_nonzero() of -0.0 is false.

  • a Bool true is true; Bool false is false.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true iff the sole element compares != 0.

Raises¶

  • if numel() != 1 (too many elements, or an empty Series)

  • if the Series is undefined

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_nonzero() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. Zero is false; any other value is true. A [1] vector works just like a scalar.

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "make_series(0.0):   " << pluss::make_series(0.0).is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "make_series(3.0):   " << pluss::make_series(3.0).is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "make_series({5.0}): " << pluss::make_series({5.0}).is_nonzero() << "\n";

Output¶

make_series(0.0):   false
make_series(3.0):   true
make_series({5.0}): true

Example 2. The comparison is literally != 0 — with the IEEE consequences.

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "NaN:   " << pluss::make_series(std::nan("")).is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "-0.0:  " << pluss::make_series(-0.0).is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "true:  " << pluss::make_series(true).is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "false: " << pluss::make_series(false).is_nonzero() << "\n";

Output¶

NaN:   true
-0.0:  false
true:  true
false: false

NaN is “nonzero” because it is not equal to 0 (it is not equal to anything). If you mean “is this a real, present number”, test isnan first.

Example 3. More than one element raises — it does not test just the first.

try {
  pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0}).is_nonzero();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

is_nonzero: expected a Series with exactly one element

Example 4. An empty Series raises too — numel() == 0 is not one element.

try {
  pluss::series::zeros({0}).is_nonzero();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

is_nonzero: expected a Series with exactly one element

Example 5. The intended pattern for a multi-value condition: reduce explicitly, then collapse.

auto pred = pluss::make_series({0.2, 0.9, 0.5});
auto all_above = pred.gt(0.1).all();       // one-element Bool Series
auto any_above = pred.gt(0.8).any();
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "all > 0.1? " << all_above.is_nonzero() << "\n"
          << "any > 0.8? " << any_above.is_nonzero() << "\n";

Output¶

all > 0.1? true
any > 0.8? true

all() / any() do the reduction you actually mean; is_nonzero() just turns their one-element result into a branchable bool.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The exactly one element rule is by rank and size: a [1] vector passes, a [2] vector and every empty Series raise.

  • NaN counts as nonzero (NaN != 0). Filter with isnan first if that is not what you want.

  • -0.0 counts as zero.

  • Never use it as a stand-in for all() / any() — it cannot reduce, it can only collapse a result that is already a single value.

Summary¶

is_nonzero() turns a one-element Series into a bool:

  • requires numel() == 1 (scalar or [1]); anything else, and every empty Series, raises

  • the test is value != 0 — NaN → true, -0.0 → false

  • pair with all() / any() to branch on a multi-value condition

See Also¶

  • Series::all / Series::any: the reductions to run before is_nonzero() when the condition has more than one value.

  • Series::numel: the count is_nonzero() insists is 1.

  • Series::isnan: distinguish a real value from the NaN that is_nonzero() reports as nonzero.
